prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It was there, the elemental center, All the time. Eternally present, repeating itself Like seasons, where the times and dates For swallows and household fires are written down, The grouse are counted, the quotas of stocked rainbows. All that love of order, for its own sake. Only the hill-farms, and the high sheep country Above politics—the enormous relief Up there, as the dialect names of skies Return, along with their clouds, and the old knowledge Opens the mind again. To dream, to just potter In the yard, to fiddle with local stations In the kitchen, where news that is no news Finally, at last, fills up the years With pure existence. Lit from beneath The fields are evenings long, the tree by the house Where Vladimir and Estragon kept vigil With the stillness of commando and insurgent Frightens no one. Slow through the air A heron, shouldering aside the weight of the world, Is making for its colonies, coevals In a state plantation . . . Nowhere but here In the high right hand of Ireland, do the weather fronts Give way so slowly, to such ambivalent light.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: All, Eternally, Like

outputs.L1:
It was there—the elemental center—all the time:  
eternally present, repeating itself like the seasons,  
where the times and dates for swallows and household fires  
are written down, the grouse counted,  
the quotas of stocked rainbows recorded.  
All that love of order for its own sake.

Only the hill farms and the high sheep country  
stand above politics—the enormous relief  
up there, as the dialect names of skies return  
along with their clouds, and the old knowledge  
opens the mind again. To dream, merely to potter  
in the yard, to fiddle with local stations  
in the kitchen, where news that is no news  
finally, at last, fills the years  
with pure existence.

Lit from beneath,  
the fields are long evenings; the tree by the house  
where Vladimir and Estragon kept vigil,  
with the stillness of commando and insurgent,  
frightens no one. Slowly, through the air,  
a heron, shouldering aside the weight of the world,  
makes for its colonies, its coevals  
on a state plantation . . .

Nowhere but here,  
in the high right hand of Ireland, do the weather fronts  
give way so slowly to such ambivalent light.
outputs.L2:
The primal core had always been there, enduring forever and circling back like the seasons. In it were recorded the appointed days for swallows and domestic hearths, the tallies of grouse, and the permitted numbers of introduced rainbow trout—order cherished simply because it was order.

Yet the upland farms and sheep-grazing heights stood beyond politics, offering immense release. There, the dialect words for different skies returned with the clouds, and ancient understanding reopened the mind. One could dream, linger over small tasks in the yard, or tune the kitchen radio from one local station to another, while reports that scarcely counted as news at last allowed the years to accumulate as sheer being.

Evening seemed to illuminate the fields from below. Beside the house stood the tree beneath which Vladimir and Estragon had waited, motionless as commandos or rebels, though it frightened nobody. A heron moved slowly across the sky, bearing away the world’s heaviness as it headed toward its fellow birds in colonies on a state-owned farm.

Only here, in Ireland’s elevated northeastern corner, did weather systems retreat with such hesitation into light so uncertain and divided.
outputs.L3:
The natural world is portrayed as an eternal, elemental center, shaped by the recurring seasons and by patterns that reveal themselves only through patient observation. In the hill farms and high sheep country, life follows rhythms older than political divisions or administrative systems. These remote landscapes offer a profound escape from politics and from the constraints of imposed order, replacing human conflict with the steadier authority of weather, terrain, animals, and time.

Local dialect, weather lore, and traditional knowledge deepen this connection to place. The names given to winds, fields, birds, and changing conditions preserve ways of seeing that might otherwise be lost. Such knowledge reopens the mind, encouraging a fuller awareness of existence and of the intimate relationship between people and their surroundings. Ordinary rural activities—tending livestock, repairing boundaries, watching the sky—and apparently uneventful local news give shape to the passing years. Through them, life becomes an experience of peaceful, unadorned being rather than a sequence of dramatic events.

The landscape of northern Ireland is therefore defined less by spectacle than by stillness and endurance. Wildlife persists across generations, weather fronts move slowly over hills and fields, and the light remains uniquely ambivalent: at once clear and shadowed, gentle and austere. In this quiet world, nature provides continuity, allowing human life to be understood as part of a larger and more enduring order.
outputs.L4:
The poem sets the pressures of modern life against the slower, elemental rhythms of rural Ireland. Contemporary existence appears regulated by clocks, institutions, public anxieties, and recurring political conflict. Its routines promise order, yet they also narrow experience and burden the mind. News, argument, and historical tension create a world in which attention is continually claimed by forces beyond the individual’s control.

Against this atmosphere, the poem turns toward the high country. Seasonal imagery places human concerns within larger cycles of darkness and growth, hardship and renewal. Weather, animals, fields, roads, and changing light are not merely decorative features of the landscape; they offer another way of understanding time. Pastoral scenes reveal an existence shaped by work, memory, and close observation, while local language preserves forms of knowledge that formal or urban culture may overlook. The land becomes a living archive, carrying the habits and perceptions of earlier generations.

This rural world is not presented as a simple escape or an untouched paradise. Its light is slow and ambivalent, capable of exposing difficulty as well as offering consolation. The countryside contains isolation, labor, age, and the weight of history. Yet its very resistance to easy idealization makes its restorative power convincing. Relief comes not from denying political turmoil or modern pressures, but from seeing them in a wider frame—one governed by seasons, weather, bodily life, and inherited understanding.

Literary allusion deepens this movement between present experience and cultural memory. The poem enters into conversation with earlier writers and traditions, suggesting that renewal can occur through language as well as landscape. Familiar words, remembered voices, and ordinary rural details reconnect the speaker with a continuity larger than the immediate moment.

In the high country, the mind therefore begins to open again. Everyday existence—walking, watching the weather, noticing animals, listening to local speech—becomes a source of knowledge and release. The world’s burdens do not disappear, but they become more bearable. By returning attention to elemental light, seasonal change, and ancestral wisdom, the poem discovers an enduring form of relief: a renewal grounded not in transcendence, but in the patient realities of place.
outputs.L5:
**All, Eternally, Like**

All that we love leaves a trace—a quiet warmth in an empty room, a familiar song carried by the wind. Nothing remains unchanged, yet some moments feel eternal.

We move through life like rivers toward the sea, gathering memories along the way. Faces fade, seasons turn, and years disappear, but love returns in unexpected forms: a kindness, a dream, a hand reaching for ours.

Perhaps eternity is not endless time. Perhaps it is a single moment remembered so deeply that it never truly ends.

And so we carry all of it—eternally, like light traveling through the dark.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about the rural highlands of Northern Ireland, contrasting timeless pastoral life with politics and modern bureaucracy.
counterfactuals.output:
Above the lough, the hills keep their old counsel—  
heather darkening under rain,  
sheep moving like scraps of cloud  
caught on the wire.

A farmer opens the byre at dawn.  
His hands know weather  
better than any forecast,  
know the weight of a gate swollen in winter,  
the small, warm thunder of milk in a pail.

Down the lane, stones remember  
names no map can settle.  
Orange lilies flare beside a wall;  
a chapel bell crosses the valley  
and meets, somewhere in mist,  
the measured silence of a meetinghouse.

For years, men drew borders  
through sentences, through fields,  
through the middle of a neighbour’s name.  
Flags climbed lampposts.  
Paint spoke sharply on kerbstones.  
The hills said nothing,  
having outlived other colours.

Now the post arrives  
with forms for livestock movement,  
grant applications, compliance notices,  
boxes too small for the truth:

How many acres?  
Which jurisdiction?  
Tick one tradition.  
Describe the river  
in block capitals.

At the kitchen table  
a woman searches for a password  
while turf settles red in the stove.  
The broadband fails.  
Rain enters the yard sideways.  
Somewhere in an office  
a clean blue screen insists  
the land is incomplete.

But evening lowers itself gently  
over Antrim, Tyrone, Fermanagh—  
over hedges stitched by generations,  
over bog cotton, ruined cottages,  
tractors ticking cool beneath the shed.

Cattle breathe along the fence.  
A curlew lifts its unfinished question.  
The farmer closes the gate  
with the same loop of rope  
his father used,

and beyond the files, the votes,  
the signatures waiting in triplicate,  
the mountain keeps no minutes,  
the river recognises no department,  
and the grass, indifferent and faithful,  
rises through every line  
we draw.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a meditative Irish landscape poem featuring hill farms, sheep country, local radio, changing weather, and an allusion to Vladimir and Estragon.
counterfactuals.output:
**Waiting Country**

Morning loosens slowly over the hill farms,  
stone walls surfacing from mist  
like old thoughts returned.

In the sheep country, ewes move  
through rush and heather,  
small grey clouds grazing the earth,  
their lambs calling into the wind.

From a kitchen radio, low on the sill,  
the county news drifts out—  
a funeral, a match postponed,  
rain approaching from the west—  
then a fiddle tune, bright as a stream  
finding tin beneath a gate.

Weather rehearses every season:  
sun on the wet fields,  
hail rattling the byre,  
blue distances opening briefly  
beyond the black shoulders of the hills.

At the crossroads, two bare hawthorns  
lean together like Vladimir and Estragon,  
keeping their long appointment  
with no one, or with evening.

And still the land waits without waiting:  
peat darkening under rain,  
sheep bells thinning into dusk,  
a tractor’s lamp climbing homeward.

Night gathers each farm by name.  
The radio murmurs on.  
Above the silent bog, one star appears—  
not an answer,  
but enough light to remain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you create a literary poem in which a speaker finds “pure existence” and relief from politics in the traditional rhythms of country life?
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn, the field rehearses no debate.  
Mist lifts its quiet banners from the rye;  
the rooster, punctual and absolute,  
announces only light.

I leave the wireless murmuring in the house—  
its borders, votes, and iron weather—  
and follow where the bucket’s silver arc  
descends into the well.

Here, every task is older than opinion:  
to split the ash, to mend the leaning gate,  
to carry feed beneath the patient gaze  
of cattle in the byre.

The scythe keeps time along the meadow’s edge,  
a breathing measure: sweep and step, sweep and step.  
Larks rise like loosened notes. The earth receives  
each falling stem without applause.

At noon, bread cools upon a wooden board;  
beans simmer with the summer’s savory.  
A clock ticks softly, not toward victory,  
but toward the evening meal.

And I, who wore the clamor like a coat,  
stand bare-armed in the ordinary sun,  
my hands made honest by the scent of soil,  
my name unnecessary.

This is not innocence. Beyond the hills  
the loud world sharpens all its hungry claims.  
But here the mare leans warmly to her foal,  
and rain begins on slate.

For one clear hour, beneath the barn’s dark beams,  
I ask no age to save me or be saved.  
I hear the swallows stitching dusk to dusk  
and find pure existence:

woodsmoke, hoofbeat, water drawn from stone—  
the faithful grammar of the small and near;  
night coming on, the lamp wick trimmed,  
the whole earth breathing without argument.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, atmospheric poem set in the “high right hand of Ireland,” using images of swallows, household fires, grouse, stocked trout, a heron, and slowly clearing weather fronts.
counterfactuals.output:
### Weather in the High Right Hand

In the high right hand of Ireland  
the hills keep counsel under wool-grey rain,  
each field a darkened pane, each stone  
holding the cold like an old grievance.

Swallows stitch the eaves to evening,  
black needles through a torn blue seam;  
below them, household fires awaken—  
turf-smoke, ash-breath, kettles beginning  
their small, iron psalms.

On the heathered shoulder, grouse  
burst from cover with a clatter of wings,  
red sparks shaken out of the bog.  
The stocked trout lie deep in the lough,  
dim coins under peat-brown water,  
waiting for light to find them.

A heron stands in the flooded meadow,  
one grey thought that will not move,  
while rain fronts loosen over the Sperrins,  
their battalions thinning west by west.

Then distances return: a gate, a steeple,  
the wet white backs of sheep;  
and, beyond the glass, the whole country  
slowly lifting its face from weather—

chimneys breathing, swallows veering,  
the heron opening its ancient wings  
as the last cloud drags its shadow  
off the high, clenched hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a modern pastoral poem with long flowing lines, understated political tension, regional dialect and knowledge, and a Beckett-inspired tree beside a farmhouse.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Tree at Carrickglass**

Beside the farmhouse an ash stands rehearsing its one black gesture, though half its crown is gone to dieback, half to the west wind worrying the same old question through it.  

It has the look of a tree that was told to wait and, being no fool, rooted itself there by the byre, where the gutter drips and the swallows stitch dusk to the rafters.  

“Sure it’ll come,” my father says, meaning rain, or money, or the lad with the part for the Massey, delayed again somewhere beyond the invisible line.  

Across the drumlin the new mast blinks red above the chapel, and every field has signal now except the lower meadow, where sedge and rush keep their own counsel.  

We turn the cattle after milking, soft-mouthed beasts shouldering through clover, while slurry darkens the cut ground and a curlew’s thin cry goes unanswered.  

On the lane, a lorry idles at the old checkpoint lay-by, though there is no checkpoint, no hut, no soldier—only nettles, broken tarmac, and room enough to remember.  

The driver leans out: “Is this road for Monaghan?” and Mam says, “Aye, if they haven’t moved it,” then laughs the small laugh people use around a truth.  

Indoors the kettle clicks; the broadband drops; a minister speaks without sound on the kitchen screen, his mouth opening and closing like a gate badly hung.  

No one complains much. The hens go picking among bolts and blue twine, the collie sleeps beneath the quad, rain travels sideways over three jurisdictions of sky.  

At evening I stand by the ash, its last leaves turning their pale undersides toward weather, and ask nothing that could be entered on a form.  

From the farmhouse comes the scrape of chairs, the Angelus, then someone saying, “Come on in, hi, you’ll perish out there,” as if perishing were merely another local shower.  

Still the tree waits beside the whitewashed wall, spare as a promise no party signed, holding one rook, one torn bag, and the whole dim country lightly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
